extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science; scientifically literate general readers
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length treatment of the scope and limits of scientific method across physical, mathematical, biological, mental, and social sciences, arguing where scientific inference is reliable, where speculation is inevitable, and where methods fail. It evaluates when laws, mathematics, observation, and theory can be trusted and where contingency, complexity, or metaphysics intervene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust theories only within their empirical data
rubrics_metrics.description: We can seldom trust our best-established theories far from their data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author repeatedly warns against extrapolating well-confirmed theories outside the domain of their observations; when reasoning far from empirical data we enter speculation and should be cautious about strong inferences (e.g., about the ultimate fate or origin of the universe).

rubrics_metrics.name: Law is compatible with extreme diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Law is not inconsistent with extreme diversity, and constant variety and ever-progressing change is the real outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate the existence of scientific laws with predictability of uniform outcomes; even strict laws can coexist with great diversity of phenomena and historical contingency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid negative inference about prior existence from present beginnings
rubrics_metrics.description: We have no right to interpret our experience negatively, so as to infer that because the present state of things began at a particular time, there was no previous existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the present physical state appears to have a beginning (e.g., heated material in a finite region), it's illegitimate to infer 'no past' without further evidence; alternative hypotheses (e.g., cyclic or bounded media) must be considered though some may be empirically inaccessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value and limits of speculative hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Speculations (such as Rankine's bounded ether) may be practically incapable of verification by observation, but they have value in drawing attention to the finiteness of our knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize speculative hypotheses as useful for highlighting conceptual limits while marking them as practically unverifiable; they should not be treated as established science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supply of new and unexplained phenomena is divergent
rubrics_metrics.description: The supply of new and unexplained facts is divergent in extent, so that the more we have explained, the more there is to explain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject the idea that science approaches a point of completeness; historical examples (laws of gases, later exceptions) show that generalisation often opens up further questions and new domains for inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: General laws are only approximately true; exceptions drive research
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalisations (e.g., isomorphism in crystallography or gas laws) are only approximately true, and divergences peculiar to each substance remain unexplained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating the adequacy of a law, note its approximate nature and treat unexplained exceptions as legitimate and valuable targets for further investigation rather than dismissing them as noise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical power is limited relative to the problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Do the powers of the highest human intellect bear a finite ratio to the things which are to be understood and calculated? Mathematical writers often omit to point out that what they do is but an infinitely small part of what might be done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be sceptical of claims that mathematics makes a science 'complete'; many physical problems exceed current mathematical methods (e.g., molecular theory, complex dynamical systems), and solved textbook problems are a tiny, special subset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coarseness of observation limits what can be theorised
rubrics_metrics.description: The rude character of our observations prevents us from being aware of the greater number of effects and actions in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for observational limitations when forming theories; lack of detection can hide important phenomena, and apparent explanatory success may be partial because instruments and methods are coarse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solvable problems are special; many natural problems are intractable
rubrics_metrics.description: The problems which are solved in our mathematical books consist of a small selection of those which happen from peculiar conditions to be solvable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that many real-world physical and social problems (three-body problem, glacier motion) are effectively insoluble with present methods, so do not generalise success on toy/special cases to all problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical epistemic limits persist even under determinism
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the motion of every particle encoded all past events (Babbage's imagery), we lack the capacity to 'read' such records; practical epistemic limits remain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between theoretical determinism and practical knowability; absence of principled unpredictability does not imply epistemic accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited applicability of scientific method to mental and social phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who attempt to establish social or moral sciences soon become aware that they are dealing with subjects of enormous perplexity; political economy and moral science involve functions so complex that scientific method makes little progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise caution applying the methods of physical sciences directly to social/moral domains; complexities, interdependencies, and individual agencies make precise mathematical treatment impracticable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impracticability of a predictive science of history
rubrics_metrics.description: A science of history in the true sense of the term is an absurd notion; a nation is an organic whole and small accidental causes may produce vast historical effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating attempts to produce laws of history, give weight to contingency, leadership, and small-scale accidents; predictive aspiration for history is misguided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolutionary theory explains general principles but not historical particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: The theories of evolution and natural selection are two of the most probable hypotheses for the origin of living forms, but they 'give a complete explanation of no single living form' and cannot show why things are as they are rather than other possible forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat evolutionary theory as powerful for unifying many facts yet limited in accounting for unique historical outcomes; accept its probabilistic/hypothetical character and its tendency to generate further questions rather than final explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolutionary explanation does not exclude design or final causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Granting the main features of Darwin and Spencer, I cannot admit that the theory of evolution will destroy theology; laws do not determine precise magnitudes, and ultimate form may be influenced by original acts or hidden determinants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reasoning about teleology or design, acknowledge that general natural laws need not preclude design-like interpretations of particular complex outcomes; retain openness to metaphysical or theological considerations when empirical laws are underdeterminate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postulate hidden determinants when uniform causes yield diverse effects
rubrics_metrics.description: If protoplasm or the germ appears chemically the same but produces widely different organisms, there must be a hidden constitution determining the extremely different results (Agassiz's point).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In explanatory practice, if ostensibly identical causes yield systematically different outcomes, prefer positing additional hidden structure/constitution rather than concluding pure chance or identical mechanism suffices.
